title: The fulfillment of time and the manner of departure
english: And I have brought her to their ruler, that is, the Word ruling over them, in order to praise her; for this was the purpose of the holy Abraham, to bring them joyfully. [Genesis 12:12: And there fell upon Abram a dark and great fear concerning the suns.]

But Abram, beholding divine sights, was seized by a fear befitting perfection. Note that a dark ecstasy fell upon him concerning the suns, signifying the progress of the Word by the passing of the day of his present state, so that another progress of blessing might be received by him as it comes upon him, according to which it was said: 'I will fulfill him with length of days,' [Genesis 25:15] not necessarily promising him long life, but clearly progress in illuminations. Therefore 'ecstasy' falls upon him; and ecstasy is not like madness, but is wonder and the translation from the visible to the invisible. For the apostle says: 'Whether then we are beside ourselves, or whether we are in our right minds' [2 Cor 5:13], not declaring that we have learned from God, but that, even if we become outside of human things through contemplation, we do this through God, just as David says: 'I said in my ecstasy: Every man is a liar' [Ps 52:6]; for having become ecstatic, he says concerning men that they are liars, he himself no longer being a man because of the communion of the Holy Spirit, but being another of those concerning whom it was said: 'For where there is strife and jealousy among you, are you not humans and walking according to human ways?' [Gal 5:15]. While Abram is in ecstasy, a dark fear falls upon him, not participating in darkness but in uncertainty and not knowing readily; such a great fear does not happen to small men. And since instead of uncertainty darkness is often taken, it is said: 'And he set darkness in his hiding place' [Ps 18:11]; and in truth, the contemplation and comprehension of super-abundant dogmas instills a gloom upon the great, and falls upon such people a divine fear with reverence.

And it was said to Abram: 'Knowing you shall know that your seed shall be a stranger in a land not its own, and they shall enslave them and afflict them for four hundred years; and the nation, which they shall serve, I will judge; and after these things they shall come out this way with much spoil.' [Genesis 15:13-14] The sojourning into Egypt...

The word foretells it; for they did not dwell as strangers being their own, having served Pharaoh and having been much ill-treated by him and the Egyptians. It does not contend with what is written there in Exodus; for there it is said: 'After four hundred and thirty years the power of the Lord went out from the land of Egypt' (Exodus 12:40), here it says 'after forty'; but it must be understood that it was not said that they went out upon the completion of the four hundred years, but after four hundred years, which the thirty [years] make manifest. And the 'I will judge the nation whom they shall serve' (Exodus 12:3) has reached its outcome according to what is written in Exodus; for He brought upon them ten-fold plagues, and they sank at last like lead in much water. But also 'with much baggage' (Exodus 12:36) they have gone out, as history shows, from which we are instructed that, even if God ill-treats someone in time, He does not do this differently, but for a good end.

If the word also alludes to the sojourning of the saints, consider this. 'And you shall go to your fathers in peace, having been nourished in a good old age; but in the fourth generation they shall return here, for the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet full' (Genesis 15:15-16). It is apparent from the immediate text that he is foretelling to him the departure from life. And for edification, these things might be said. The wise man departs from life in peace, but the one sinning has confused thoughts and has a troubled soul; and just as one is received in death, so he will be judged. The one having prepared peace for himself from this place, he departs in peace, but the one having trouble and confused thoughts toward this, he will be judged. This is shown from what is in Ecclesiastes: 'Wherever the wood falls, there it remains' (Ecclesiastes 9:7). This does not have this meaning in history; for it is not always that wherever wood falls, there it remains; for often it is moved; but it is clear that the man is what is signified in enigma through the wood, so he will be judged as he is found.

Therefore, fittingly, Abraham will depart to the fathers being pleasing to God, sharing the same promise; for 'the firstfruits' [are] 'Christ, then those of Christ.' And even for the righteous, the promise and the dwelling are different; for there are many dwellings with the Father. Thus, he will depart to the fathers according to the Spirit, being diligent in the...

title: The Fire of the Covenant and the Divided Pieces
english: A son is like a father in manner, even if the father is weak in the flesh. Regarding Abraham, it is said concerning those from him that 'in the fourth generation they shall turn away from this place' (Gen 15:16), signifying the inheritance of the land. Because of this, it is said that after 'four hundred years' (Gen 15:16) the turning away shall be, because the Amorites had not yet filled up their sins, by which they would afterward be judged, so that after they are judged, they might become inhabitants of that land.

For God brings punishments with measure and timing, being long-suffering until the time of retribution arrives. Similar and constructive to this is what is said in the Gospel: 'Then Jesus began to upbraid the cities in which most of his powers had come to pass, because they did not repent: Woe to you, Chorazin; woe to you, Bethsaida, for if in Tyre and Sidon the powers that happened in you had happened, long ago they would have repented in sackcloth and ashes' (Matt 11:20-22). To this someone asks: How is it then that they did not repent, if indeed they were repenting, but rather they were completed there where they did not repent? And we say that the Son of God is wisdom, who also did these things; for knowing the hidden things, he knew that those repenting were not making a true repentance, and because of this the powers did not occur there.

And it is appropriate to say concerning them: it is better for them not to have known the truth than to have known and to have turned back to what is behind. Thus he did not do the extraordinary things for Tyre and Sidon; for it was to be easy for them to repent. Since those among whom the movement occurred did not have a soul recognizable to the judge, which required the demonstration of signs, he did this so that these might be without defense, and those [Amorites] might not cause more harm at an unseasonable time. And if this has been said excessively by the Savior to rebuke those who saw the signs and did not repent—and indeed this way is didactic—one should consider it. For the long-suffering and goodness of the Judge is shown in awaiting the fulfillment of the sins of the Amorites, after having reproved and exhorted and everything that leads to recognition, before God brings the punishment, just as it happened to Pharaoh.
For often, being subject to punishment and being deemed worthy of forgiveness, he brought upon himself through his own hardness of heart the final condemnation.

And when the sun had gone toward the west, a flame became, and behold, a smoking oven and torches of fire, which passed between the divided pieces. The clarity of the saying would be shown thus: concerning the sun already setting, 'a flame became' and 'a smoking oven' appeared, and 'also torches of fire, which passed between the divided pieces,' both burning and lighting the place so as to see the patriarch's actions and to show the symbols more divinely, which is necessary to investigate. And this is to be noted, that not only when a covenant is being made did fire appear, but also through Moses the law is given upon fire; for they saw the fire, but not seeing the one speaking, they heard the things having been legislated. But it was suggested through these things that such things might be. Since the law has struggle and punishment, having been given in the midst of the fire, it was evident that it brings burning to some and illumination to others. For the fire has a twofold power, lighting and burning at once; so the law having been given burns those who fall away from it, and illuminates its guardians. So also here torches and smoke appeared; and smoke is a completion and as a following-up of fire having appeared, but a flame became first. We say therefore that in such a difficulty for the one dividing the practical things, there must be illumination from God and fear, as is indicated by the oven, so that all things may be accomplished according to the right word.

On that day the Lord God established a covenant with Abram, saying: 'To your seed I will give this land from the river of Egypt even to the great river Euphrates, the Kenites, and the following.' Of the torches passing through the divided pieces, the covenant was being confirmed, the God saying: 'To your seed I will give this land,' and he also traces out the extent of the land. And it is necessary, according to the previously stated things, to understand the land being given to the seed as being given to the one according to the Holy Spirit. This also the Savior promises to those who have been made upright in meekness. This is a fitting promise to the true children and not to the...

title: The Pedagogy of Ascent
english: Through succession to all. For 'the children of the flesh are not these children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as seed' (Genesis 17:19). For he who does the works of it is his child. And also well [is] 'from river to river'; for the virtue which is the due promise to the seed is that which is in the middle of flowing things, not being parts of the flowing things, but their boundaries; for if any virtue should become external to it, these things immediately encounter it. And if this has been said to the virtuous one because of the lying in wait of trials, you will understand, it being in the middle of those distressing [things] and overcoming them.

But Sarah the wife of Abram did not bear him children. And she had an Egyptian handmaid, whose name was Hagar. And Sarah said to Abram: 'Behold, the Lord has closed up on me the not-to-bear-children; go therefore to my handmaid, so that I may make children from her.' And Abram obeyed the voice of Sarah. The apostle led these to the two covenants by the law of allegory; and since the literal has also come to pass, it is also worthy to be seen. The holy ones lived together thus, not to hunt pleasures but for the sake of children. For such a tradition is brought about concerning them, that they only had intercourse with women when they had a time of conception; neither while nursing nor while feeding the infant, nor while pregnant, did they have intercourse; for in none of these times did they consider union to be appropriate.

And Jacob also confirms the tradition; for having tested in much time that Rachel did not accept to bear children, he no longer approached her; and she, thinking that if he approached her, she would bear, was saying: 'Give me children, or if not, kill me.' For he did not know that Jacob was not a potter, but was seeking union as if the holy one had ceased for the said reason, so that he might not labor in vain. And he said to her: 'Am I instead God to you, who has deprived you of the fruit of the womb?' (Genesis 29:31). And Sarah, being wise and holy, knowing for much time that through intercourse she had not received according to the belly, abstained from the fellowship with him, and since she knew that he would have children following [him], she gave her handmaid to him as a wife concubine. The temperance and also the abundance of Sarah and of Abram are shown.
The lack of passion comes not from one's own impulse, but through offspring produced by a woman. The explicit teaching is indeed useful, as we have explained.

The logic of ascent is smoothed out by using the pattern of the blessed Paul, who led the two women toward the two covenants; using this method in other matters, he led Sarah toward perfect virtue and philosophy, she being a married woman, free and noble, and living according to the laws; and virtue lives with the wise according to the laws, so that she may bring forth divine offspring from herself. For 'Wisdom' 'bears prudence to a man' (Prov 31:10), and it is said toward the pious and holy: 'Your wife shall be like a fruitful vine, your children like olive shoots around your table' (Ps 128:3). Thus the man who fears the Lord shall be blessed toward perfect virtue.

Sarah is led toward the spiritual, while Hagar the handmaid, the Egypt, is signified by Philo as the preliminary exercises and by Paul as the shadow. For it is impossible to grasp any of the spiritual or high notions without the shadow according to the letter or the introductory training; for one must first produce offspring from the lesser things. According to the shadow, they were immersing themselves, performing Pascha sensuously and circumcising themselves physically, being led by these things toward 'offering a sacrifice of praise to God' (Heb 13:15), which is the property of the free.

Since it is a matter of diligence for the wise to make room for the greater things, virtue proposes to use the introductory things first with a divine aim and to bring forth offspring from them. For since he who is now approaching virtue is not able to grasp perfection and thus bring forth from it, it is assumed that he first clothes himself in the preliminary trainings, so that he may also make room for it perfectly, if he is able.

And having taken Sarah, the wife of Abram, Hagar the Egyptian, his own handmaid, after ten years of living with Abram in the land of Canaan, she gave her to Abram her husband as a wife, and went in to Hagar, and conceived (Gen 16:3).
